title: Lecture 8-26-2026
text:
Chemistry can be defined as the science that deals with materials of the universe and the changes these materials undergo.
Commonly referred to as the “central” science.

Examples of Chemical Change - Baking soda and vinegar react to fizz - Car engine burning gasoline - Food being digested by the body


Science is a framework for gaining and organizing knowledge.(See Scientific Method).


State the problem and collect data (make observations)
Quantitative: How much of something. (Has units, such as pounds or inches) Qualitiative: This quality of something. (Does not include numbers and units)
Example

An apple is red (qualitative)
It is raining outside (qualitative)
The car is travelling at 60 MPS (quantitative)
A solution has a density of 1.2 g/mL (quantitative)
A cheeseburger is delicious (qualitative, and opinionated)
The meal costs $11.00 (quantitative)




Creating a Hypothesis:
A Hypothesis is a possible explanation for the observation, in order for it to be science we musts be able to test the hypothesis.



Perform Experiments:

An experiment is something we do to test hypothesis.




Once we have a set of consisting hypothesis that agree with our various observations, you can assemble the hypotheses into a theory often called a model.
A theory can be an interpretation, which is a possible explanation of why nature behaves in a particular way.

title: Lecture 8-26-2026
text:
Scientific Notation

Scientific notation is a method for making very large or very small numbers more compact and easier to write.

Expresses a number as a product of a number between 1 and 10 and the appropriate power of 10.


Ergo
\[
93,000,000 = 9.3 * 10,000,000 = 9.3 * 10^7
\]
93 million here becomes a number between 1 and 10 and we use the exponent applied to 10 to represent how many decimal places were moved to provide our 9.3 base.
A positive power represents a number greater than one and a negative power represents a number less than 0. Use the decimal place to figure out how large the exponent over 10 should be.
Ergo \(0.0072\) can be represented as \(7.2*10^-3\)

title: Lecture 8-26-2026
text:
Examples Problems
Write the following numbers in scientific notation:

0.00000756 = \(7.56*10^-5\)
13500 = \(1.35*10^4\)
56000000 = \(5.6*10^7\)
0.0089 = \(8.9*10^2\)

Convert the following numbers into the standard notation:
\(9.1*10^3\)
This can be simplified to \(9.1 * 1000 = 9100\)
Ergo \(9.1*10^3=9100\)
\(3.56*10^-4 = 0.000356\)
\(1.10*10^5 = 110,000\)
So all that being said the exponent over 10 can be used to represent how many places the decimal point should move left (negative) or right (positive).

title: Lecture 8-28-2026
text:
The numbers recorded in a measurement (all of the certain figures and uncertain figures).

Significant Figures: Any measurement involving an estimate and thus is uncertain to some extent.
We signify the degree of certainty for a particular measurement by the number of significant figures we record, e.g. 2.85 has 3 significant figures.




Non-zero integers always count as significant figures
Zeros have some rules

Leading zeros are zeros that preceded all of the non-zero digits, these do not count as a significant figures.
e.g. 0.0025 only has 2 significant figures (the two and five).
The numbers after non-zero digits do count as significant figures.
Zeros that fall between non-zero digits are significant figures.(Captive zero)

Trailing Zeros

100 has only one sig fig, but 100. has three sig figs.

Scientific Notation Clarifies Sig Figs


\(1*10^2 = 100\) but clarifies in Scientific notation that only one sig fig.
\(1.0*10^=100\) has two sig figs.
\(62,000\) only has two sig figs but \(62,000.\) (with the decimal point) represents a calculation that specifies all digits as significant.


Exact numbers

Found when you count physically like there are 5 apples.
Assumed to have unlimited sig figs.






For multiplication and division, the number of sigfigs in the result is the same as that in the measurement with the smallest number of sig figs.
For addition or subtraction, the limiting term is the one with the smallest sig figs.

Examples
\[
4.0 + 18.004-0.915 \newline
\] The smallest sig fig comes from 4.0 so our solutions should only have two sig figs. \[
4.0 + 18.004-0.915=22.919 \newline
\textsf{rounding to two sig figs} \newline
22.9
\]




To change one unit to another we use a conversion factor.

A conversion factor is a ratio of the two parts of the statement that relates two units.

Example: Convert 2.85cm to inches
\[
2.85 cm * \frac{1 in}{2.54} = \frac{2.85in}{2.54} = 1.12in
\]

We choose a conversion factor that cancels the units we want to discard and leaves the units we want in the result.

Convert 3.41 L to mL
\[
3.41L * \frac{10000mL}{1L} \newline \newline
\frac{3.41*1000}{1}=3410mL
\]
8522 cm to km
\[
8522 cm * \frac{1m}{100cm} * \frac{1km}{1000} = 0.08522 km
\]
Convert to meters first and convert the meters conversion to kilometers. You could also just take the true difference between kilometers and centimeter directly and skip the meter conversion.
\[
9.30*10^3 km * \frac{1000}{1} = 9.3*10^6 meters
\]
0.015 g to mg
\[
0.015g * \frac{1}{1*10^-2} = 15mg
\]

title: Lecture 9-2-2026
text:
A Physical change involves a change in one or more physical properties of a substance but no change in the composition of that substance. E.g. Water freezing.



A chemical change transforms a substance into one or more new substances.

Also referred to as a reaction

E.g. Electrolysis of Water:

Water decomposes to hydrogen and oxygen gases when you apply an electric current to water.
Cooking an egg is technically a chemical change because when you cool down the egg to it’s original temperature it doesn’t return to it’s original physical state.




Elements only contain one type of atom. They cannot be broken down in other substances by chemical means.

Examples:

iron \(\mathrm{Fe}\)
aluminum \(\mathrm{Al}\)
oxygen \(\mathrm{O}\)
hydrogen \(\mathrm{H}\)





Compounds are substances that contain two or more kinds of atoms.
Examples:

Water, \(\mathrm{H_2O}\)
glucose, \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\)

A Molecule contains atoms bound together in a particular way.
Di-atomic elements are naturally paired with one more of their own atom to be stable.
Stable diatomic elements:
\[
\mathrm{Cr_2}\mathrm{I_2}\mathrm{N_2}\mathrm{Cl_2}\mathrm{H_2}\mathrm{O_2}\mathrm{F_2}
\]



A mixture has a variable composition.
Air is a mixutre because it can be seperated into its various component gases.
Heterogenous mixtures can be visually seen to be seperate.
Homogenous mixtures components cannot be easily seen by their individual components.


Has the same properties throughout.

Table salt and water form a homogenous mixture.
Homogeneous mixtures are also known as solutions.




When you can visually see the difference in mixture. There are said to be different properties in different parts of the mixture.

Sand and water form a heterogeneous mixture.





A pure substance always has the same composition.
Pure substances can also be compounds, e.g. a glass full of (water)\(\space \mathrm{H_20}\)

Types of Pure Substances
Puresubstances are either:

Elements
Compounds

Elements cannot be broken down chemically into simpler substances.
Compounds can be broken down chemically into elements.

title: Lecture 8-30-2026
text:
Fahrenheit


Used in GB and US, used in most engineering sciences.


Celsius


Used in Canada and Europe, used in physical life sciences in most countries.


Kelvin


Absolute temp scale

A lot of these temperatures are based on when water boils and when it freezes.
Celsius - \(0^\circ\) for example at \(0^\circ\) is when water freezes.
Kelvin helps relate temperature to the amount of energy (or average energy in a system).


\(T_{\circ{C}} + 273 = T_\mathbf{K}\)

title: Lecture 8-30-2026
text:
Physical Properties
The characterisitics of a substance that do not involve changing to another substance.
Examples: * Odor * Color * Volume * Density * Melting Point
Basically anything used to describe some substance.

How a substance reacts to another substance. Or the ability for a substance’s ability to change to a different substance.
Examples: * Acidity * Flammability * Reactivity
